name: Tara Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I'm the data and local economy reporter at the Valley Ledger, which is an online-only news site for our region, about thirty staff. I start the day with a dashboard I built that pulls new planning applications, business closures and council spending from public websites overnight. Then I pick the two or three things that look odd and start phoning people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most about that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Finding the story nobody else noticed because it was buried on page forty of a spreadsheet. Last spring I spotted that one landlord had filed for eleven house-in-multiple-occupation licences on the same street, and that became a three-part series. That kind of thing still gives me a buzz.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Meetings about traffic and audience numbers, mostly. Also chasing comment from press officers who reply at 4:58 on a Friday. I use AI tools every day, for sorting documents and checking my numbers, so the grind part of my job is already smaller than it was three years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something cheeky like, 'Turns out the robots just wanted to help with the spreadsheets.' At work I'd say the tools are useful but they were never going to do the reporting for us. Nobody would be very surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a plateau is fine for me. I've already built the AI into how I work, so I keep the time savings and nobody else catches up much. The Ledger is one of the few local news outlets actually growing its subscriptions, so my job feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much would change. I'd keep building my document tools and maybe teach a lunchtime session for the newsroom, because a few colleagues still paste things into a chatbot and hope. I'd keep saving the way I do now and maybe finally take that month off to walk the coast path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit smug maybe. It would be nice to stop hearing that the end is coming every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job or money that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot, honestly. I have about ten months of costs saved and a small flat my grandmother helped me buy, so rent can't push me around. If the Ledger went bust tomorrow, I could probably walk into the comms team at the university or the health trust within a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you teach in that lunchtime session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the sports desk and the two subeditors. One of them, Gareth (a subeditor in his forties), checks every name and date by hand because he doesn't trust the tools. I'd show him how to use the AI to flag possible mistakes and then check those himself.

say: I'd joke that **the robots** just wanted to help with the spreadsheets.
I'd tell colleagues AI was **useful** but never going to do the reporting.
think: I think a plateau suits me, because I've **already built** AI into my work.
The Ledger is **growing subscriptions**, so my job feels solid.
do: Keep building my **document tools** for planning and spending records.
Run a **lunchtime session** teaching colleagues to use AI properly.
Take the **month off** to walk the coast path.
feel: I'd feel **calm** and a little smug, glad the warnings of doom stopped.
S0.quote: If the Ledger went bust tomorrow, I could probably walk into the comms team at the university or the health trust within a month.
fieldNote: Tara's security rests on **savings, a flat** and a growing employer, not on AI staying weak.
She treats AI as **her own advantage** over slower colleagues.
Her instinct is to **teach others**, especially an older subeditor who checks everything by hand.

steps.text: Keep the overnight dashboard pulling planning and spending records
Add an AI checker that flags names and dates for the subeditors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: this is good for reporting if we use the time to dig deeper. I'd probably write a column for the Ledger saying local news can do more with fewer routine chores. Online I'd be the optimistic one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well and other people wouldn't. The rewrites of council press releases, the event listings, the sports results, that's half the newsroom's output and software does it. I'd likely end up running the team that builds and checks the tools, and some of my friends would end up out of work. That bit doesn't sit well with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd pitch the editor a proper role, something like news tools lead, with a pay rise. I'd build a checking system so every AI-written brief gets a human sign-off before it goes up. I'd also do a short online course in data engineering, about eight hundred in fees, so I'm not just the person who knows prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly for other people. For me it's exciting, and I feel a bit guilty that it's exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some friends would end up out of work. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Priya does listings and events for the Ledger. That's exactly the kind of work that gets automated first, and Priya would be lost without a newsroom around her. I'd try to bring Priya onto the tools team as a checker, if I had any say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk the tools team gets cut too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure, eventually. Once the tools are built, you need fewer people to run them. But in this picture there's time, and I'd rather be the one building the news tools than the one being replaced by them.

say: I'd say this is **good for reporting** if we use the time to dig deeper.
I'd write a **Ledger column** arguing local news can do more with fewer chores.
think: I think **I'd do well** while other people in the newsroom wouldn't.
Listings, briefs and results are **half the output**, and software does them.
I feel uneasy that **my friends** would end up out of work.
do: Pitch the editor a **news tools lead** role with a pay rise.
Build a **human sign-off** step for every AI-written brief.
Take an **online course** in data engineering for about eight hundred in fees.
feel: I'd feel **excited** for myself and **guilty** about being excited.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the one building the news tools than the one being replaced by them.
fieldNote: Tara expects to **gain** from this scenario, and her unease is about friends, not herself.
She'd try to pull **Priya, a listings writer**, onto the tools team as a checker.
She accepts the tools team **shrinks later** but trusts the time to adjust.

steps.text: Pitch the editor a news tools lead role with a pay rise
Take an online course costing about eight hundred in data engineering
Build a sign-off checklist for every AI-written brief

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need honest conversations in newsrooms right now, not in two years. I'd probably write that the public still deserves reporting it can check, by a named person. I wouldn't pretend I had the answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years kills my advantage. My edge is that I'm quicker with the tools than most reporters, but if the AI can find the odd planning application and write the series by itself, being quick with tools doesn't matter. What's left is the phone calls and the trust, and I'm not sure the Ledger would pay for that alone. Robots coming three years later means nothing for me, because there's nothing hands-on in my job except typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the Ledger, because they'd still need someone to check what goes out for a while. I'd stop any big spending, keep my ten months of savings untouched and add to them. I'd start talking to the local university about their applied AI unit, since they'll need people who understand both newsrooms and these systems, even if only for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, properly. I've always been the one ahead of the change, and with AGI in two years I'd just be standing in it like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a flat and savings. Doesn't that take some of the edge off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a lot. I won't lose my home and I can pay bills for most of a year. What it doesn't fix is not knowing what I'd be doing at thirty, and that's the part that would keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad, who's an accountant, that we're in the same boat now. He always said journalism was risky and accountancy was safe. In this picture, both of us are facing it at the same time.

say: I'd say newsrooms need **honest conversations** now, not in two years.
I'd write that people still deserve reporting **by a named person** they can check.
think: I think two years **wipes out my edge**, which is being quick with tools.
What's left is **phone calls and trust**, and the Ledger might not pay for that alone.
The **robot delay** means nothing to me, since my job is all thinking work.
do: Keep working at the Ledger as a **checker** while they still need one.
Freeze big spending and **add to** my ten months of savings.
Approach the university's **applied AI unit** about a role.
feel: I'd feel **properly anxious**, standing in the change instead of ahead of it.
S2.quote: I've always been the one ahead of the change, and with AGI in two years I'd just be standing in it like everyone else.
fieldNote: Tara's whole **sense of security** comes from being early, and fast AGI removes that.
Her **flat and savings** protect her home, but not her sense of direction.
She noted that her **dad's accountancy** job is now as exposed as hers.

steps.text: Stay at the Ledger as the person who checks AI copy
Leave the flat fund untouched and save more each month
Ask the university's applied AI unit about a role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if newsrooms use it, and a waste if they don't. I'd probably organise a meetup for regional reporters to share what's working. Publicly I'd sound practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can ride my advantage for maybe three and then jump. I'd get very good at running AI newsrooms while it still pays, then move into something with people at the centre before 2031. I'm 27, so I'd be 32 at the end of it, which is young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the tools lead job in year one and save hard, maybe forty percent of my pay. By year two or three I'd start a part-time master's in something like public policy or mediation. And I'd start a small paid newsletter on regional housing data, because owning a little audience of my own is worth having whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, alert way. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the newsletter survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not as a data product, no. But people might pay to hear from a reporter they know and trust, the way they buy bread from a local baker. I'd treat it as an experiment, not a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said forty percent. What gets cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, mostly, and the new laptop I've been eyeing. I'd keep the coast walk. Some things you don't put off.

say: I'd say five years is **a gift** if newsrooms use it.
I'd organise a **meetup** for regional reporters to share what works.
think: I think I can **ride my advantage** for about three years, then jump.
At **32** I'd still be young enough to start again.
do: Take the **tools lead** job in year one and save **forty percent** of pay.
Start a part-time **master's** in public policy or mediation by year three.
Launch a small **paid newsletter** on regional housing data.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy but alert**, because this is something I can plan for.
S3.quote: People might pay to hear from a reporter they know and trust, the way they buy bread from a local baker.
fieldNote: The extra three years lets Tara **plan a jump** instead of reacting to one.
She's honest that the **newsletter** may not survive AGI and calls it an experiment.
Her **age** is her main source of comfort in this picture.

steps.text: Save forty percent of pay by cutting eating out and the laptop
Start a part-time master's in public policy by year three
Launch a paid newsletter on regional housing data

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives local news a real shot at reinventing itself. I'd be the one at conferences saying let's experiment now rather than wait. People would probably find me a bit much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still end up out of a reporting job by 2036. But ten years is a career in itself. I could spend six years building tools and a reputation, and then step into something new with real savings behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the tools lead job and build the Ledger's whole AI system over the first few years. I'd keep saving and put some into a stock index fund, since the AI companies will grow. I'd start the newsletter as a side project too, and somewhere around year five I'd pick my next field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly curious. It's the same ending, just with time to choose how I meet it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of you that would hope it doesn't happen at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small part, yes. I love the moment of finding a story in a spreadsheet, and that moment would be gone. But I'd rather be honest with myself than hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger reporters joining now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new reporter to learn the tools in year one and to build trust with real people in every year after that. Trust is the one thing I can't see software owning.

say: I'd say ten years gives local news **a real shot** at reinventing itself.
I'd tell conferences to **experiment now** rather than wait.
think: I think I'd still be out of a **reporting job** by 2036.
Ten years is **a career in itself**, with time to build savings and a name.
do: Build the Ledger's **AI system** as tools lead over the first few years.
Put some savings into a **stock index fund**.
Pick my **next field** around year five.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy but curious**, with time to choose how I meet the change.
S4.quote: I'd tell a new reporter to learn the tools in year one and to build trust with real people in every year after that.
fieldNote: Tara admits she'd **miss the thrill** of finding stories in data.
With ten years she sees a **full career** ahead before the change lands.
Her advice to younger reporters, **trust over tools**, is also her own plan.

steps.text: Build the Ledger's AI newsroom system as tools lead
Put part of my savings into a stock index fund
Run the housing data newsletter as a side project

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the one thing I'm good at being early with. What would help is newsrooms being honest about plans, and some funding for local reporting as a public good, because I think people will still want a human they can hold to account.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to friendships at work. If I'm the one building the tools that replace my friends, that's going to be awkward at the pub on Friday. Nobody talks about the social side of this.

headlineQuote: If I'm the one building the tools that replace my friends, that's going to be awkward at the pub on Friday.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old data reporter** at an online regional news site, with a flat and ten months saved.
She's **curious and quick** with AI, using it every day to sort documents and check numbers.
In the milder pictures she expects to **gain** and feels guilty about friends who won't.
With **AGI by 2028** her edge disappears and she feels anxious about her direction, not her home.
With more time she plans to **ride, save and jump**, and starts a small newsletter.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it removes her advantage of being early with the tools.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest plans** from newsrooms and **public funding** for local reporting people can hold to account.
